thread.title: DeWine vetoes mail-in photo ID, submetering bills - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: DeWine vetoes mail-in photo ID, submetering bills - NewsBreak

author: DANNY ELDREDGE
title: DeWine vetoes mail-in photo ID, submetering bills - NewsBreak
text:
By DANNY ELDREDGE ,
2 hours ago
COLUMBUS — Legislation requiring voters to show a photo ID for mail-in ballots was vetoed by Gov. Mike DeWine on Wednesday night.
The governor also vetoed a bill that would have specified that submetering companies are not public utilities but are subject to other types of regulations.
Both the photo ID measure, House Bill 472, and the submetering legislation, House Bill 173, were passed during marathon voting sessions ahead of state lawmakers’ summer recess.
House Bill 472
In his veto message, Mr. DeWine said H.B. 472 is unnecessary because Ohio already does an excellent job running elections.
"House Bill 472 would not discourage fraud, would not add any real security, and would create an additional and significant burden for Ohioans who vote by mail,” the governor said.
Mr. DeWine also pointed to the opposition from Republicans and Democrats in the Ohio Association of Election Officials.
“This bipartisan group agrees that Ohio’s election system is strong and 'is widely regarded as one of the most secure and well-administered in the nation. The success of that system is the result of careful planning, adequate resources, bipartisan administration, and the ability of elections officials to implement changes thoughtfully and effectively,’” the governor said.
Mr. DeWine said the legislature did not make a compelling case to make yet another change to Ohio’s election laws, noting H.B. 472 does not give election officials any new tools to fight fraud.
“The purpose of a photo ID is to match the picture on the ID with the face of the person presenting the ID. This makes logical sense when votes are cast in person,” he said. “However, requiring the photo ID for the mail-in ballot process does not provide election officials with any opportunity to verify if the ID picture matches the face of the voter and thereby serves as no additional verification of the voter’s true identity.”
Mr. DeWine said the bill would place additional burdens on many voters, but especially senior citizens, individuals living in long-term care facilities, voters with mobility issues, and people with limited access to technology.
“Absentee voters would now be required either to access a new online portal and learn how to use it to upload images of their photo ID, or make and print photocopies of their photo ID, or affirm they are exempt from these requirements via a specific form that does not yet exist but would need to be created by the secretary of state,” he said, noting these could create barriers if they are not carefully designed and clearly understood.
“While on paper, one can make the case that there is a pathway for absentee voters to overcome the hurdles to voting that this bill creates, if the net result is that a number of voters will be deterred from making the attempt to vote, that result is hurtful -- not helpful -- to our efforts to include all of our citizens in the most basic act that involves them in our democratic process,” Mr. DeWine said.
The governor also criticized the lack of funding in the bill, saying the Ohio Secretary of State’s Office and county boards of elections would incur significant new administrative costs.
“In other words, this is an unfunded mandate both for the Ohio secretary of state and for every county in Ohio,” he said.
The Ohio Organizing Collaborative held a rally outside the Statehouse on Wednesday, urging the governor to veto the legislation.
Mary O’Boyle, leader of the Clinton County chapter of Parents United for Public Schools, said H.B. 472 originally would have made voting more accessible when it was simply about waiving document fees for individuals experiencing homelessness.
“But several senators decided to use this House bill to actually suppress voting power,” Ms. O’Boyle said. “Why are you making it harder for people to vote? What is your motive? What are you afraid of?”
Ohio Senate President Rob McColley (R., Napoleon) said photo ID laws are supported by the vast majority of Ohio voters.
“It is disappointing the governor would oppose such a common-sense election security bill when Democrat-controlled states such as Virginia and Hawaii have repealed their photo ID laws,” Mr. McColley said. “H.B. 472 — when combined with this fall's constitutional amendment requiring photo identification to vote — would have given Ohioans the confidence to know that their election system was the most secure in the country.”
House Bill 173
The governor said vetoing H.B. 173 was in the public interest because the bill would have legitimized a “fundamentally-flawed” submetering model.
He pointed to a recent decision from the Ohio Supreme Court finding that submetering companies are public utilities that must be regulated by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio.
“House Bill 173 would exempt submetering companies from the definition of a public utility, although the Public Utilities Commission would still retain oversight authority,” Mr. DeWine said. “However, while this bill does contain some consumer protections, they are not as robust as those afforded to customers of Ohio’s electric utilities.”
The governor said H.B. 173 would not allow submetering customers to choose their own provider of retail electric generation service, and it would not allow submetering customers to participate in the Percentage of Income Payment Programs offered by public utilities.
“Further ... H.B. 173 would permit submetering companies to charge tenants for electric service provided to common areas such as hallways, community rooms, and outdoor lighting,” he said. “As a consumer protection principle, tenants should only be individually billed for the electric service usage for which they are individually responsible.”
The governor said a more traditional submetering model that does not harm customers could continue in Ohio without H.B. 173.
“That traditional model, that is still widely used, has the property owner or a third-party billing company calculating the utility cost based on both actual usage and local utility rates and then issuing a bill to the tenant,” he said. “For that work, the third-party billing company is paid a fee by the property owner. The billing company does not buy the electricity at wholesale price and sell it at retail price.”
Other bills signed on Wednesday
The following bills were among those signed by the governor on Wednesday:
● Senate Bill 273, which requires the Ohio State Highway Patrol to provide a security detail to the lieutenant governor, governor-elect, lieutenant governor-elect, and certain eligible gubernatorial candidates and immediate family at the governor’s direction. The bill provides $10 million to help fund the required security operations.
● House Bill 479, a budget corrections bill that creates the Post-Traumatic Stress Fund Commission and appropriates $1.5 billion in surplus fiscal year 2026 tax revenue for various purposes. However, the governor issued a line-item veto of a provision that would have terminated previously appropriated funding to the Outdoor Recreation Council of Appalachia.
● Senate Bill 106, which declares that electric vehicle charging stations are competitive retail electric services that consumers may obtain from any supplier.
summary: "House Bill 472 would not discourage fraud, would not add any real security, and would create an additional and significant burden for Ohioans who vote by mail,” the governor said. The success of that system is the result of careful planning, adequate resources, bipartisan administration, and the ability of elections officials to implement changes thoughtfully and effectively,’” the governor said. The governor also criticized the lack of funding in the bill, saying the Ohio Secretary of State’s Office and county boards of elections would incur significant new administrative costs.
